en: Preface to the Commentary on the *Ālambanaparīkṣā-vṛtti*:
This *Commentary on the Ālambanaparīkṣā* is the exposition by the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla of Master Dignāga’s *Ālambanaparīkṣā*.
Master Dignāga profoundly exhausted the nature of conditions and thoroughly penetrated the source of vision; he established the truth and eliminated error, clarifying the mind.
There is no external object. The Sautrāntikas and others maintain that the aggregation of external material atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitutes the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

[The author] refutes them, stating that their positions are both unreasonable because they lack one of the two essential factors. The Bodhisattva sets forth his own doctrine: internal matter appears as if it were external and serves as the objective condition for consciousness.

This is because he admits that its aspect (*ākāra*) resides within consciousness and that it is capable of producing consciousness. The ancient Mahāyāna masters, however, were brief regarding the notion of "carrying along" (*sākṣāt-karaṇa*).
Thus, when fundamental wisdom takes *tathatā* (suchness) as its object, there appears to be a flaw regarding its status as an *ālambana-pratyaya* (object-condition).

However, for the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna, which does not admit of transformation or representation (*nirbhāsa*), the definition of the object-condition would fail to apply when visual consciousness perceives form. For the Bodhisattva, this principle is well-established;
thus both factors [of the causal complex] are complete. By understanding it in this way, one realizes that there are no objects external to the mind, and that all phenomena perceived are merely such.
This is the perspective of the mind. Yet, while the text is concise, its meaning is vast; what it contains is profound and subtle.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla brought forth its remaining depths, fully excavating its mysterious mysteries.

He composed a commentary to propagate its intent, casting the radiance of correct principle and overflowing with the waves of the ocean of meaning, causing poisonous intellects to withdraw and the flames of heterodoxy to be extinguished. Furthermore, the translated text is remarkable for its stylistic uniqueness.

The text is perilous; readers find it difficult to penetrate. A man from the high plateau of Mount Da-guangming (Great Radiance), whose mastery of doctrinal studies was rigorous and exhaustive, has long researched this scripture.

He has performed a subtle analysis of its extraordinary principles and recorded them in notes. This is like tracing a river to its source, whereby all its winding tributaries become clearly understood;
or like felling a tree at its root, whereby all its tangled branches fall away together. Thus, the meanings that had been stalled for a thousand years—
Dantonglang was one whom scholars delighted to behold; he was of profound benefit to the Dharma-gate. Through this superior man, one sees Dharmapāla;
through Dharmapāla, one sees Dignāga—just as seeing one’s own face in a mirror.
Preface to the *Commentary on the Exposition of the Object-Condition* composed by the sick layman Wang Ye.
Regarding the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*): it is the third of the four conditions. This single factor possesses two functional capacities.

First, it can produce consciousness; second, it acts as the object-condition (*ālambana*). "Object" (*viṣaya*) is another name for the objective field, while "producing consciousness" is the definition of a condition (*pratyaya*);
thus it is called both the "object-condition" and simply a "condition. Now, since the three realms are mind-only, there are fundamentally no external objects possessing substantial characteristics.

It was only when the five sciences arose in the world that the designations of "internal" and "external" emerged. Therefore, Dignāga, out of compassion for those submerged in various heterodox attachments, examined the texts and summarized them.

In accordance with the meaning, he composed this treatise. Dharmapāla brought forth its hidden and subtle profound principles; by categorizing the sections and analyzing the logic, he produced this commentary.

The author of the treatise established *anumāna* (inference) as the guiding principle to subdue the doubts of those with heterodox and inverted views, to clarify internal form (*rūpa*), and to reveal the obscure path.

His precious thoughts flew like the wind, perfectly matching the eloquence of pouring from one vessel into another; the waves of the false ford were stilled, relying upon the power of his tongue-rolling silence.

Through this capability, he caused the followers of other schools to all bow their bodies in respectful submission. From this point forward, the concealed meanings of the Mahāyāna began to display their brilliance and radiate their light.
Those who expound his works observe the profound gateway of the Threefold Division (*triskandha*) and push open the heavy barrier of the Fivefold Division (*pañcavastu*).

Gazing at the heavens and surveying the sea, they grieve that scholars cannot fathom its height and depth; looking back to the vast Han era and the distant source, they lament that those of future generations will have no way to know it.

Thus, the Bodhisattva’s divine faculties were clearly manifest and his discursive arguments were refined. As he pointed toward the fundamental causes and conditions, the poisonous wisdoms were gathered in while the flames of insight increased;
as he discerned benefits and harms, the river of craving was exhausted and he was bathed in the waves of grace.

Although the ultimate Way was thus brilliantly illuminated and its flying radiance shone like the sun, it originated from the arrival of the Sanskrit texts from the West, which were then translated according to their intent; the phrasing and diction were exquisite.
This is a humble work produced by the translator. In the past, when I examined this commentary, my eyes were like those facing a blank wall and my mouth could not form a single phrase.

This was because the source of its diction is so refined and concise, while the ocean of its meaning is so profound and vast; though I remained close to the desk and its texts, I ultimately could not compose even a single word of my own.
Fortunately, relying upon the power of the Bodhisattva’s great compassionate vow, and meeting with the accumulated merit of myself and others such as Yu, I have suddenly been able to...
Having personally heard the sound of the Brahma-voice, he was filled with leaping joy as if he had received a prophecy.

He then investigated treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, as well as sūtras such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*. Whenever he encountered points where the underlying intent was coherent, he recorded them in writing for the sake of easy consultation, titling his work the *Commentary on the Treatise on the Object-condition (Ālambanapratyaya-viṣayaviniścaya-śāstra)*.
Written on the day before Qingming in the year of Jiyou (1609) of the Wanli era by the śramaṇa Mingyu of Fuci Temple in Western Sichuan,
at the Yuhua Jingshe in Jinling; with section headings provided.

The structural framework of this treatise serves as its guiding principle; through these topical divisions (*kośa*), one first comes to understand how the thematic threads are interwoven and how the logical force of the arguments unfolds and converges.

Thus, the essential teaching of "Mind-Only" becomes vividly clear to both mind and eye. When the masters of antiquity categorized the scriptures, they invariably employed a three-part structure. However, regarding the *Ālambanaparīkṣā*, only a single part can be maintained:

it lacks the introductory section explaining the origin of the work at the beginning, and it lacks the concluding section on the propagation of the teaching at the end. This is consistent with the nature of a commentary (*vyākhyā*).
Regarding the treatise, there are two parts. The first verse specifically clarifies the reasons for composing the treatise; therefore, it is designated as the introductory section (*nidāna*).

Within the main body (*śarīra*), the topical outline follows the structure established by the *Vyākhyāyukti*. It is divided into two general sections: first, refuting the attachments of outsiders who hold external form to be the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*);
second, elucidating our own school’s position, which establishes internal form as the objective condition. This is the general outline of these sections.

Regarding this "Commentary on the Investigation of the Object-Condition": it is the observation of the objective sphere (*ālambana-viṣaya*), which necessarily possesses the capacity to give rise to consciousness.

Discussing it by way of its conditions (*pratyaya*): discourse (*vāda*) is insufficient to exhaust its details; therefore, it is further supplemented with an explanation (*vyākhyā*). "Explanation" means the elucidation of meaning;

"discourse" means the differentiation of meaning; "condition" means the sense of a close friend; "object-condition" (*ālambana*) means the sense of having an objective domain; "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) means the sense of observation, that is, the sense of illuminating the objective domain with wisdom.
This refers to the fact that ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle do not penetrate the principle of Mind-Only, and thus falsely cling [to external objects].
They maintain that there are real objects external to the mind, which are either atoms (*paramāṇu*) or composites (*saṃghāta*) formed by those atoms;

they each separately grasp these as the meaning of the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Therefore, the Master composed this treatise to cause them to investigate that the faculties and their objects are nothing but mind, so that they do not fall into the dense forest of false views. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "As for the object-condition, it is said that if..."
There is a phenomenon (dharma) that carries its own characteristic (sanimitta). It is either associated with the mind (cittasamprayukta). The commentary explains:

"That which is 'a phenomenon' must be a substantial entity; this is the name for the objective essence (ālambana). 'Carrying its own characteristic' refers to the image-aspect (nimittabhāga), which is called the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).

When the characteristic and the essence are spoken of together, they are termed the object-condition. The character 'carrying' (dai) belongs to the mind; 'own' (ji) belongs to the essential substance; and 'characteristic' (xiang) is the image-aspect."

This refers to the cognizing mind. When it takes an object as its focal point (*ālambana*), it brings forth its own image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) which carries the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of that object.

"Carrying" has two meanings: first, "transformative carrying," which refers to the eight consciousnesses having an essential nature that serves as their remote objective condition (*parokṣa-ālambana-pratyaya*).
Taking this objective realm possessing substance as its essence, there arises an appearance that resembles that essence; this is called "transformation-carrying" (bian-dai).
Second is "clamping-carrying" (xie-dai), which refers to all actual image-parts (*nimittabhāga*) that are immediate objective conditions (*ālambanapratyaya*).
Because these image-parts are not separate from the cognizing mind, the cognizing mind clamps onto these image-parts and perceives them; this is called "clamping" (xie).

Regarding "carrying" (*ādāna*), the self-aspect (*svākāra*) also has two meanings. First, the aspect of appearance (*nimittākāra*): this refers to the self-aspect that carries a semblance of the objective substance (*ālambana*).

Because the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) resembles the essential body of the original substance, it is called the "remote object-condition" (*viprakṛṣṭālambanapratyaya*). Second, the aspect of essence (*svabhāvākāra*).
That is to say, it carries along with it its own aspect (nimitta-bhāga) which is the objective referent;

because this objective aspect is not separate from the substance of the cognizing subject, it is called the "directly apprehended object-condition" (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*). Regarding the phrase "the mind or its associated [mental factors]," this distinguishes the result of the object-condition.
Taking the object as the condition is the cause, and that which arises—the mind and mental factors—is the result. "Mind" here refers to the eight consciousnesses.
The mind-king (*cittarāja*) is associated with fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*), which may arise or not arise; hence the further use of the word "or" (*vā*).

The above concludes the explanation of the four characters *guān suǒyuán yuán* (contemplating the object-condition). Regarding the fifth character, *lùn* (treatise/discussion), the *Weishi kaimeng* (Introduction to Consciousness-Only) states:

"It instructs students, discriminates between nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), stimulates and clarifies the ultimate tenets, adorns the convergence of meanings, and establishes a model for future generations."
It is called a *lun* (treatise). Sixth, regarding the character for "explanation" (*shì*). "Explanation" means to understand. It refers to thorough analysis and interpretation;

it dispels doubt to achieve understanding, scatters turbidity to preserve clarity, and sets aside the verbal expression to embrace the meaning—thus it is called an "explanation. Seventh, regarding the character for "record" (*jì*).
It has three meanings: memory, discernment, and recording. This term "record" (*jì*) refers to compiling and assembling [the material] into a codex to prevent its loss.
Because it is forgotten, it is not a *vyākaraṇa* (prediction). It is merely called "recording" (*jì*) because it takes up memory and documentation. The explanation of the title is complete.
△ Below, the text is divided into sections; first is the Introduction (*nidāna*).

If one says that [this teaching] enables those with poisonous wisdom to become persons of wisdom, so that their insight may be rendered utterly clear and their evils eliminated—having paid homage, one should contemplate its meaning:
phenomena do not arise in isolation; they arise only by depending upon objects. Sentient beings are shrouded by poisonous wisdom and fail to comprehend these objects.
The principle that "emptiness exists within the mind" is the initial movement of the Bodhisattva’s great compassion, intended to cause others to observe their own minds and attain self-awakening.
As for those referred to as "poisonous intellectuals," they are people whose wisdom is not clear.

Because their wisdom is unclear, they grasp at objects external to the mind, thereby harming the *dharmakāya* and wounding the life-force of wisdom; thus, they are called "poisonous intellectuals. Among the three poisons, this refers to the poison of delusion (*moha*).
It is thus complete. A portion of the poison of greed is taken up in order to grasp external objects; because it belongs to the category of greed, why would it not be a portion of hatred? It is said:
since it coexists with greed, one is stained by attachment toward the object and does not feel aversion toward it; therefore, there is no hatred.

How does this harm the Dharma-body or wound the life-force of wisdom? It is said: that [ignorance] clings to external forms as the conditions for the arising of consciousness, and further clings to them as its...
The objects of conditions are the境 (objects) of the mind; through the mind’s false conceptualization, afflictions arise.

Because afflictions arise, they obscure the true meaning and obstruct the eye of noble wisdom. Is this not the very life-force of wisdom within the Dharma-body? Therefore, one knows that the poison of ignorance is a harm no small matter.
To cause these people’s wisdom to become utterly clear and to eliminate their transgressions, one must necessarily rely on the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only).

Examining the correct principle with discernment, I prostrate to the Triple Gem and contemplate its meaning. △ The first section, the introduction, is concluded. Below are the two sections of the main body.
Regarding the text of the treatise itself, it consists solely of seven categories; all other categories follow the divisions established in the commentary.
Generally, when a title is followed by the characters "lun" (論), these are from the text of the treatise itself. When it is titled "shi" (釋) or lacks the title "shi," [it refers to the commentary].
The term "it is said" (*yue zhe*) serves to explain the treatise as a whole. Now, regarding the first part of the main body of the text (*zhengzong*), it is divided into two sections:

first, the refutation of others' attachments; second, the elucidation of our own school’s tenets. The first section is further divided into two: first, the general indication; second, the specific refutation.

The first of these is further divided into two: first, the general discussion; second, the specific analysis. The first of these is further divided into three: first, a discussion on the internal consciousness that acts as the perceiver (*neng yuan*); second, a discussion on the object perceived (*suo yuan*).
External objects. These three refute their [erroneous] attachments. Furthermore, this is divided into two parts. First, a restatement of the brief explanation from the root treatise.

The treatise says: Those who wish to maintain that the five consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness, take external form as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), either hold that atoms (*paramāṇu*) exist as substantial entities because they can produce consciousness, or they hold that it is the composite (*saṃghāta*) [of atoms], since when consciousness arises, it bears the image of that [object].
"Because it is a characteristic.

The commentary explains: For those who assert that there are consciousnesses such as visual consciousness, the objects that are discarded and the objects that are gathered are either abandoned or grasped;
because this is the fruit of observation, the nature of the objects thus abandoned and the cause of perversion are what are being demonstrated.

Regarding those who assert that there are consciousnesses such as the visual consciousness and so forth—referring to the passage in the *Mūla-śāstra* which states, "those who wish to maintain that the five consciousnesses, such as the visual, [arise from external objects]"—the Master Hu now cites and explains this.

He says that other vehicles (i.e., non-Buddhist schools) maintain that the five consciousnesses, such as the visual, take external forms (*bāhya-rūpa*) as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
These "external forms" consist of two types as they are conceived by those [schools]: atoms (*paramāṇu*) and their aggregations (*saṃghāta*).
The atom (paramāṇu) has no substantial entity; it is established through the analytical observation of form.

If one were to divide Mount Sumeru into seven parts and take one part, and further divide that into seven, continuing this process of division until reaching the atom—therefore, Master Hu (Paramārtha) regards the atom as something to be discarded.
Since Mount Sumeru can be analyzed into atoms, atoms can likewise be combined to form Mount Sumeru.
Therefore, the Dharma Master Hugu takes "conjunction" (*saṃghāta*) as the object to be subsumed. Regarding what is either abandoned or accepted:
this refers to other schools who either accept atoms (*paramāṇu*) while abandoning conjunction, or accept conjunction while abandoning atoms.
The establishment of the grasped object is the fruit of their investigative wisdom; the entity that is abandoned is the object not accepted by those other schools.
Furthermore, the causes of inversion are matters adhered to by other schools; it is for this reason that they are presented here.
Regarding the "causes of inversion," this is a critique of their false attribution of causality to what is not a cause. Part One: The brief explanation of the root treatise is concluded.

Below, Part Two concerns the differentiation of the perceiving subject (*ālambaka*), which is divided into three sections. The first section discusses that which is subsumed under the term "equal" (*sama*).
The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) here includes the five types of consciousness that depend upon the sense faculties as accepted by others;

for others invariably maintain that these take real entities (*dravyasat*) as their objects. This is not the case for mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because it is not invariably so. It is therefore accepted as existing conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*).

Because of [the existence of] chariots and so forth, even if one were to grant that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes real entities as its objects in some limited respect, it is still able to take a representation resembling the object as its objective support, even when the actual object is absent.
Thus, once it is established that for the visual consciousness and the others, the object is not separate from the representation, [the argument is proven].
Only then would it be established. For this reason, no great effort is expended here [to refute that view].
This [argument] refutes the tenet of other schools which maintains that the sense-faculties and consciousnesses have different objects of cognition than the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
In this context, the word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to the term "eye etc. (*cakṣur-ādi*) found in our own treatise. Master Dharmapāla explains: "The word 'etc. here means to include..."

He [the Master] permits that the five types of consciousness depend upon their respective sense-faculties. Why is this? Because others maintain that these [consciousnesses] invariably take the aggregation of atoms as a real entity (vastu) as their object.

This statement is the Dharma-master’s refutation of other schools who maintain that the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, invariably take the aggregation of atoms as a truly real object;
he asserts that this is not the case for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which does not invariably do so.
"Thus" means that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is not the same as the five [sensory] consciousnesses.
The mind does not invariably take real entities as its objects, because it is admitted that there are conventional existents (*saṃvṛtisat*), such as chariots and the like.

This explains that the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, invariably take real entities as their objective spheres, while one admits that chariots and the like are conventional existents, because one treats chariots and the like as real entities. [The opponent] asks: "The mind..."
[Question: Consciousness sometimes can also take real entities as its objects. Why do you say that this is not the case for mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)? [Answer:

Even if one were to grant that mental consciousness takes real entities as its objects to some small degree, it is still able to take the appearance resembling that consciousness [itself] as its object;

there is no separate external object apart from it. This means that when mental consciousness perceives an object, in a single moment it perceives by way of being separated from that object. Its characteristic is such.
The "semblance-aspect" refers to the shadow-like aspect that arises as a semblance of a substance upon an object through the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
To be "separated from its object" means to be separated from the actual object and to cognize only the shadow.

Regarding the phrase "not separated from the objects of the visual and other consciousnesses," this means that when the visual and other consciousnesses cognize their objects without separation, the objects so cognized are all substantially existent.
Therefore, it is known that the [position regarding] the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is not so.
Since it is not universal, once its [inconsistency] has been established, there is no need for further insistence on what the other school considers to be self-evidently logical.
Once the principle has been clearly demonstrated, what benefit is there in persisting in the claim regarding the mental consciousness?

Furthermore, the forms cognized by the wisdom resulting from habitual cultivation are certainly not the objective domain of the *cūḍika* [consciousness], because they are established exactly as they are perceived.
Here, however, we are considering only the objects of the wisdoms born of hearing, reflection, and innate attainment.

Thus, the objects apprehended by this mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) entirely become non-existent, because it cannot take its own constituent group (*sva-saṃtāna*) as an object. Moreover, it apprehends...

Because past and future things are not real entities, they are like unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). For this reason, these words include the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*).
According to other schools, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) cannot take the objects of the five consciousnesses as its domain; it only takes past and future non-real entities as its objects.

As for what is called "form cognized by resultant wisdom," this refers to the infinitesimal particles (*paramāṇu-rūpa*) within the context of conceptual meditation (*parikalpita-dhyāna*). *Tsa* (Excerpt).

"Ka" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This form is precisely the object-condition (*ālambana*) of the mental consciousness; other schools, on the contrary, claim that it is certainly not within the range of the mental consciousness.

Furthermore, regarding "that which is established according to what is seen," this means that the mental consciousness, taking the substantial form as its basis, establishes conventional designations (*nāma-pada*).
It is precisely through such false attachment that, within conceptual observation (*parikalpita-dṛṣṭi*), one analyzes [form] down to the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*). This is the correct [view].
This is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that establishes names and conventions. Even non-Buddhist schools claim that [the ultimate] is not within the range of the mental consciousness;
all such views are ignorant of the principle of the non-duality of form and mind, falsely clinging to the idea that there are real entities existing as objects external to the mind.
Now, regarding the objects of the wisdoms produced by hearing, reflection, and innate attainment: this "wisdom" refers to the sixth mental consciousness, while the "objects" refer to what is heard.
The object of reflection refers to this mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which arises from the objects heard and explained; it takes these very objects as its focal point (*ālambana*).
"Mental" means that by reflecting solely upon the objects of hearing and reflection, one gives rise to the wisdom of mental consciousness.

Furthermore, the phrase "solely reflecting" is used to demonstrate that mental consciousness takes only these objects as its conditions. Such an object of focus for this mental consciousness becomes entirely [established].
Regarding "non-existent": this refers to the fact that when one investigates consciousness with respect to higher-order conceptual designations and names, neither can serve as an object of cognition.
As for the phrase "because it cannot take its own aggregate as an object": "self" here refers to the atom (*paramāṇu*), while "aggregate" refers to a combination.

This further means that consciousness cannot take the combination of atoms as its objective domain; furthermore, because it takes past and future things as objects, which are not real entities, [it likewise cannot take them as objects]. Just as...

If it were unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), this would imply that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes the conventional (*prajñapti*) as its object and cannot take the real (*dravya*) as its object. Therefore, the conclusion below states:

"For these reasons," which includes the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*). △ The first section on what is included by the term "etc. is finished. Below, the second section discusses how the mental consciousness takes distinct objects.
If that is so, how is it that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is induced by the sense-faculty consciousnesses?

This [mental consciousness] does not arise simultaneously with its corresponding sense-faculty consciousness, nor does it arise immediately after it without any interval, because it takes form and other objects as its objective support (*ālambana*). Alternatively, it takes the present as its object;

however, this is not something that was previously apprehended by the sense-faculty consciousness. Thus, the mental consciousness is able to directly perceive the essential nature of external objects on its own. This, then—
Consequently, one would not become deaf, blind, or otherwise impaired; furthermore, this would contradict inference (*anumāna*), which establishes the existence of distinct sense faculties.
Since this [position] excludes the increase of visible form (*rūpa*) as being what is intended [by the opponent], no further consideration need be given to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

This refutes the opposing school’s position, which does not allow that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses to take the five objects as its domain.
Therefore, Master Dharmapāla asks: "If that is so, then how is it that the mental consciousness is induced by the sense-consciousnesses?"
The phrase "if that were so" refers to the meaning in the preceding chapter. It means:

This serves as an illustration to demonstrate that atoms (*paramāṇu*) lack spatial dimensions. However, when it comes to these atoms, how could they ever possess distinct shapes?
This is because the substance of an atom has no distinct characteristics. Therefore, the treatise states: "That [atom] should not..."

Therefore, it is certain that within a composite aggregate, [the object] does not exist as a real entity. This explains that although the aggregate exists...

If it is argued that because their characteristics differ, their linguistic designations differ, this statement intends to clarify that the previous claim—that "that which is not a distinct entity cannot serve as an object"—is a restatement of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

It is not already established. There are two points: admitting that there is the nature of a cause is already established; not admitting the existence of an object of cognition (*ālambana*) is not yet established.

This concludes the discussion of the preceding three sections. Furthermore, an analogy is cited to resolve this:

it clarifies that the consciousnesses of the various sense faculties do not take as their objective support (*ālambana*) the substance of the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), since it possesses no distinct form; even if there were distinctions such as jars or bowls, [the atom itself remains without such form].

Neither are they objects of the sense-consciousnesses, just like other consciousnesses. "Other consciousnesses" refers either to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) or to other sense-consciousnesses;

for when one perceives blue, there is no appearance of yellow. These four propositions restate the principle that, within the examples cited, the objects of each respective consciousness are determined.
Regarding the point that when one perceives blue, there is no appearance of yellow: this means, for instance, when visual consciousness perceives the color blue, that blue cannot become yellow;

It is certain that this consciousness cannot take [atoms] as its object through the ear-consciousness and so forth.
Although these atoms are numerous in substance, they lack differentiation; yet the sensory consciousnesses possess differentiated characteristics.

This means that because the atoms have no distinction, they cannot serve as the objects of apprehension for multiple consciousnesses, since the natures of the various consciousnesses are distinct. Thus, this is established in common.
Regarding the nature of not being a state of atomic form: according to the intent of this section, it is likewise established that atoms do not possess distinct characteristics.

this distinction of form is a concealed existence (*saṃvṛtisat*), because its nature consists in having jars and the like as its objects.

It is distinct. It is merely a covering formed by a collection; and this form of a collection is conventional, not real.
This is the correct principle (*nyāya*). Therefore it is said: "Such a correct principle ought to be established.

Verse: "Separation" (*viyoga*) means analysis (*vibhāga*). That is to say, if the objects were distinct, the cognitions produced by them would likewise be distinct;

To explain why this contradiction prevents the arising of consciousness—namely, that "this distinct shape exists as a concealed reality because it has the nature of being an object such as a jar"—it means that although the shapes of these jars and bowls differ, they exist as the concealed reality of the actual atoms. Internal matter appears as if it were external; it is accepted as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for consciousness because its aspect resides within consciousness and it is capable of producing consciousness.
Thus, although external objects do not exist, internal matter appearing as if it were an external object serves as the objective condition, and the visual and other consciousnesses are so accepted.

Because it arises bearing that image and because it is produced from it—it possesses these two meanings. Since this internal objective image is not separate from consciousness, how can it arise simultaneously with it and yet act as a condition for that consciousness?

Because they are necessarily concomitant, they also act as conditions simultaneously; or rather, because the former acts as a condition for the latter by inducing its functional capacity, the objective aspect (*viṣayākāra*) and consciousness are necessarily concomitant.
Thus, even though they arise simultaneously, the objective aspect also acts as a condition for consciousness. So say the logicians (*hetuvādins*).
If this and that are mutually concomitant in their existence or non-existence, then even though they arise simultaneously, they may still possess the relationship of cause and effect.

Alternatively, the aspect of a preceding consciousness serves as the condition for a subsequent consciousness, inducing within the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) a capacity that produces an appearance resembling its own result, thereby causing it to arise.
Because it does not contradict reason: if the five consciousnesses arise by taking only internal form as their object, how can it also be said that the eye and so forth are their conditions?
The capacity for cognition within form is reasonably termed the "five faculties"; this capacity and the objective form have been mutual causes since beginningless time.
Because consciousness can arise, one infers the existence of the faculties (*indriya*). These are merely functional capacities (*śakti*) and are not produced from external matter;

therefore, the fivefold functional capacities upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) are termed the "eye-faculty" and so forth. This is also not contrary to reason, because there is no logical distinction between a functional capacity giving rise to consciousness and the faculty itself.

Although it cannot be said that [the object] exists either in consciousness or elsewhere, because external phenomena do not exist in principle, one must certainly admit that this exists in consciousness and not elsewhere.
This faculty of the sense organ and the objective form of the external world have served as reciprocal causes for one another since beginningless time.
This means that when this capacity reaches its state of maturation, it gives rise to the five internal objective forms upon the manifesting consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).

These internal objective forms, in turn, can induce the capacities of the five sense organs upon the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*). Regarding these two types of form—the sense organs and the objects—as to whether they are identical to or different from consciousness: [they are neither identical nor different].

Alternatively, they may be neither identical nor different; one should explain them according to one's preference. Thus, it is well established by reason that these various consciousnesses have only the internal objective aspect as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The commentary states: Based on the nature of internal objects, this refers to the entities that serve as the focal points (ālambana) established by one's own school.

If one were to categorically deny the existence of any focal object, there would be the fault of contradicting worldly consensus and one's own accepted tenets, for the four types of conditions (pratyaya) are taught in the Sūtras.
Based on the essence of the internal object, this refers to the "objective aspect" (*nimittabhāga*) of form established by the Bodhisattva Dignāga.

if one were to universally negate the existence of an objective referent, there would be the fault of contradicting worldly convention and one's own accepted tenets. This means that the term "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) does not constitute a universal negation.

Regarding the objective referent (*ālambana*): the reason our own school establishes that all phenomena are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) is not to deny the existence of all phenomena, but rather to demonstrate that all phenomena are merely manifestations of the mind.

It is commonly known by the world that the five consciousnesses take the five sensory objects as their referents, and our own school likewise accepts the teaching that the eight consciousnesses arise from four conditions.
If one were to categorically negate the existence of objective referents, it would entail these two faults.
This is unavoidable; therefore, it is said that there are four kinds of causal conditions (*pratyaya*). This is because they are taught in the sutras. The four kinds are:

the direct cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). The meaning of these conditions is explained in detail in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), so I shall not cite them here at length.

all of these are the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), not the function of the five sensory consciousnesses. As for what constitutes the actual cause:

although internal form serves as the objective condition (*ālambana*), it is also truly the cause that gives rise to the consciousness, just as hair-threads and the like appear to visual consciousness.
This is used as a metaphor for the meaning that internal form appears as if it were external. That is to say, one whose eyes are fatigued sees tufts of hair appearing above a lamp;
although they appear externally upon the lamp, they actually exist due to the fatigue of the eyes.
This serves as a metaphor for how form, though appearing as if external, in reality does not depart from the transforming mind.

Although external objects do not exist—meaning that there are truly no external objects because their nature cannot be apprehended—one investigates through reasoning and finds that their own essence cannot be established as definitely existing externally.

therefore, it is not the case that atoms manifest as forms. This is like when external forms appear as if they were manifesting.
This is precisely what constitutes the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Because it is associated with that [internal] aspect (*nimitta*), the *Mūla-śāstra* states:

Regarding "as for the external": this means that when one investigates by means of the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), external form cannot be taken as an object.

Thus, it is admitted that internal form serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Even if one were to concede that those external appearances exist substantially, they are not the objects of consciousness, nor do they possess the nature of such appearances;
therefore, they are not the manifestation of atomic characteristics (*paramāṇu*). This [section] restates the prior calculation of the other vehicles regarding atoms.

The object of consciousness. The above explains that although external objects do not exist, the following concludes by revealing the nature of the *nimitta-bhāga* (the objective aspect).

As is conceived by the mind, the characteristics of the object arise accordingly. This is clarified through an analogy:

when the mental consciousness (*vijñāna*) engages in conceptualization (*vikalpa*), there arises the characteristic of an "isolated shadow" (*kevala-chāyā*) object that evolves in accordance with the consciousness. This is analogous to the "objective division" (*nimitta-bhāga*) of form.
Consciousness arises simultaneously [with its objects]; therefore, it does not depend upon external forms as its objective realm.
Furthermore, that which is conceptually grasped by the mind does not exist externally apart from consciousness; thus, these objective appearances are fundamentally not separate from consciousness.
This is what is meant by the "characteristics of internal objects.
To explain the analogy for clarifying the objective aspect of internal objects:

thus, it arises by depending upon that objective aspect. This is in the sense of "arising from.

Regarding the statement that there is a distinction based on the five meanings of the sixth [consciousness]: this means that the objective aspects of the first five [consciousnesses] arise from actual seeds and are therefore called "real."
The objective realm (*viṣaya*) is the sixth [aspect], the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective part). That which arises as an external aspect of defilement is called the "solitary shadow" (*ekacchāyā*) object;
thus, there is a distinction. First, to explain the primary meaning of the preceding five [consciousnesses]:

"Because consciousness exists without being separate from the object" means that consciousness does not obtain its cognitive object (*ālambana*) apart from the objective part (*nimitta-bhāga*). Therefore, it is only when this [objective part] exists that consciousness arises. This means that because this...

Only when there is an objective field as the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) is consciousness subsequently induced. The reason for not mentioning a "fifth" [factor] is precisely the meaning of the aforementioned "fifth sound":
it means that one does not state a claim by using a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), because the two factors are conjoined.

As for "because the two dharmas are combined," this means that within a single image-part, both the capacity to produce [consciousness] and the nature of being an object of cognition already exist; therefore, one knows this spontaneously without needing to establish a formal inference (*anumāna*).

This clarifies that the reason is logically consistent with its object (*ālambana*). It reveals the intention of the proponent (*sādhaka*) in explaining the consistency between the two aforementioned factors.
That is to say, it takes only the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) as the probans (*sādhana*);
for it is maintained that what can produce a universal characteristic as its object must necessarily be an internal object (*antarviṣaya*) in order to be established.
As for the distinction: the *piyāna* does not take external objects as its objective support; rather, it manifests them within the state of dreaming.

As it is said, there are two aspects that together constitute a single proof: the consciousness possessing that image, and the arising of that consciousness. It functions by taking these two as its objective support.
This completes the first measure.
This explains the meaning of the preceding distinctions. As for the distinction: the term "pṛthagjana" (in Sanskrit) is cited as the name for the preceding distinction;

this is translated here as the "aggregate of consciousness" (*vijñānaskandha*), which is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). It does not take external objects as its conditions, but serves as a manifestation within the state of dreaming.
This refers to the objects perceived within a dream; they are not external things, yet they can be manifested as internal objective images.
This is like saying that two kinds [of functions] constitute a single probans (*sādhana*). That is to say, it is as when one says:

"If consciousness possesses that image (*nimitta*) and that [image] is the object of this [consciousness], then on the basis of a single aspect-part (*ekākāra-bhāga*), there are two functional capacities, which are termed 'two kinds'. This refers to consciousness.

"Having that appearance, it is further produced from consciousness" means that the consciousness within a dream possesses the appearance of a dream-object, and that dream-object appearance is itself produced from consciousness.
"Depending on these two functions, they together constitute a single valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)"—the term "depending" (*yuan*) here signifies "by means of.
That is to say, by virtue of these two kinds of functions, the status of a single internal object as a valid cognition is established.

Furthermore, even granting for the sake of argument that internal aspects exist, since one perceives only the false appearance of external objects, it is said that there are no other [external] aspects.
Just as when one conceptualizes an object according to one's own mental state, the aspect of the object that is experienced is presented internally; this is taken to be the rational position.
How can that one part serve as the condition for the co-arising [of consciousness]?
Since the apprehended portion does not exist apart from consciousness, this very portion would again give rise to consciousness, thereby resulting in the fault of contradicting its own nature.

Furthermore, because it is of the same nature as that [consciousness], just like the apprehending portion, it would consequently lack the capacity to produce [consciousness] and would exist merely by virtue of external appearance.
It arises from the defiled consciousness. This means that the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the consciousness arise together;

it is not that two separate things exist simultaneously, for they possess a causal relationship like the two horns of an ox. Furthermore, it is not the case that two non-different things existing at the same time are spoken of as a compound using the term "concomitant" (*sahabhū*);
nor is it that the object is mentioned separately from the consciousness.
This refutes the internal aspect (antarākāra) as it is differentiated [from the external]. It does not share the same meaning as the internal aspect that is a portion of the object (viṣayāmśa).

Furthermore, even granting for the sake of argument that there is such an internal aspect—meaning, for instance, granting that there is the objective aspect within a dream—it is because one merely perceives the falsely existent aspect of an external object.
As for the statement that "there is no other aspect," it means that what was previously perceived as an external object now manifests as a transformation within the dreaming mind.
There is nothing else to say. To clarify further through an analogy how objects arise according to the mental projections of sentient beings:

the aspect of the object that is experienced is presented as being internal. If one considers this to be logical—that the external object is produced by the defiled consciousness—and takes it to be the principle of a real, existent objective part (*nimittabhāga*), then how can that single part serve as the condition for its own simultaneous arising?

That is to say, if one grants that dream-objects possess two functions—namely, being the object-condition (*ālambana*) and producing consciousness—one must admit they possess only the single aspect of being an object-condition.

How, then, could they serve as the condition for the production of consciousness? As for the claim that "the apprehended aspect does not exist apart from consciousness," this refutes the position that there is no object-condition.
This means that objects in the state of dreaming are merely transformations of the mental consciousness within the dream; if they were separate from the mind...

If consciousness [is such that] the objective aspect of the perceived object is inherently non-existent, then for this single portion to again give rise to consciousness would constitute the fallacy of contradicting its own nature.
This refers to the objective aspects within a dream, which originally arise as transformations of consciousness;
how could they, in turn, produce the consciousness that transforms them? If they cannot produce consciousness, they remain merely a portion of the object of cognition (*ālambana*).

Because it is an object-field (*viṣaya*), it is said: "Furthermore, since it is of the same nature as a portion of that [consciousness], just like the subjective grasping portion (*grāhakāṃśa*), the objective field would then fail to possess the nature of being produced by the subject.

This refutes the position that consciousness cannot produce [its objects]. That is to say, if one takes the objective appearances within a dream as the *ālambana-pratyaya* (object-condition), then the object arises from consciousness;
how could one then claim that the object exists prior [to consciousness] and conversely produces the subjective grasping?
Is it consciousness? That which arises from being defiled by external marks is like this: the dream-object is unreal.
This refers to the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) arising simultaneously with consciousness; this concludes the meaning of the preceding distinction.

"The former" refers to "arising from this," which means that in the root treatise, [consciousness] arises bearing those marks. This dream-object mark is precisely an analogy for the objective aspect and consciousness.
They arise simultaneously; however, the fault lies in the fact that a dream-object cannot induce the arising of consciousness. Therefore, three challenges are raised in succession below.
The first challenge states: "It is not the case that two things existing simultaneously possess the nature of cause and effect, like the two horns of an ox.

This means that this dream-object is not like the simultaneous existence of the 'seen' and the 'perceiving' (nimitta and darśana), where the object acts as the cause that induces the arising of the consciousness produced."
[This is] for the sake of the result. It is like the two horns of an ox, each of which exists as a real entity. The second objection states:
Furthermore, it is not the case that things which are non-different from one another are spoken of together using a term of association because they exist at the same time.

This is because the characteristics of dream-objects do not resemble their objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*); rather, the objects and consciousness are fundamentally non-different things that exist at the same time. Because they are identical—
The sound "not separate from the companion" is spoken in conjunction [with the preceding]. The third objection states:

Nor is it that there is a distinct object of cognition (viṣaya) apart from consciousness; for dream-objects are seen falsely based upon consciousness. Nor do internal forms (rūpa) and the cognizing consciousness exist as separate, substantially real entities.
How, then, can these be called "having the nature of companions" (addressing the question regarding the simultaneous occurrence of the aspects)? In reality, this is indeed so;

however, due to the power of the distinctions between their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are conjectured to be different and expressed as such. This is because there exists a distinction between the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) and the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).
"Thus, these consciousnesses come to have distinctions.

This answers the intent of the preceding question, clarifying that while the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is fundamentally the same, distinctions are manifested through the power of karma.
"The reality is indeed thus" answers the companion's question. The intent of that question is: since the Mahāyāna establishes *vijñapti-mātra*, [how can there be such distinctions?]
Consciousness is the fundamental tenet. Why, then, speak of "concomitants"? If one were to say they are identical, there would be two distinct dharmas.

Therefore, the answer states: in principle there is no duality; in reality, it is merely consciousness alone. Nevertheless, it is due to the power of the differentiation of its phenomenal characteristics (*nimitta*) that...
This means that upon the substance of the *ālayavijñāna*, two companion parts manifest; therefore, they are called "distinct.
As for those who conjecture them to be different and express them as such: it means that when consciousness gives rise to these two factors (*dharma*), originally they have no names.

It is only through the inference and deliberation of the Sages that they are designated as distinct as "seeing" (*darśana*) and "object-aspect" (*nimitta*), and thus expressed. Because there is this distinction between the seeing-part and the object-aspect, consequently...
Regarding the distinctions among these consciousnesses: the essence of the *ālayavijñāna* is fundamentally the one True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Due to the manifestation of diverse characteristics, the arising of distinctions within the *ālayavijñāna* is revealed. Although there are two divisions of distinction, they both originally arise from the single essence of consciousness.
Since the essence of consciousness is free from defilement, it is precisely True Suchness; therefore, it is said that "the three realms are mind-only."
"All phenomena are consciousness-only.
If this were so, then the nature of the object-condition (*ālambana*) would also be merely that which is grasped; it would not be a discriminated entity possessing an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
In that case, it would follow that the nature of the object-condition is not truly real. This would be contradictory.

Furthermore, there is this objection: If it is truly the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), and you merely establish the names "subject" (*darśana-bhāga*) and "object" (*nimitta-bhāga*) through conjecture, then the "objective aspect" (*nimitta-bhāga*) established by your Mahāyāna must be nothing but a conceptualized false attachment.
How could that which is a conceptualized false attachment possess a self-nature (*svabhāva*)? Since it lacks self-nature, your objective aspect is not real.
As for the nature of conditions (*pratyaya*): since it itself is not real, the previous refutation of the atom as a composite aggregate is rendered irrelevant.
This is because the meaning of "condition" is likewise accepted by both parties regarding other distinct objects of attachment, such as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
When consciousness of the homogeneous class (*sabhāga*) is severed, this consciousness likewise functions as a condition by way of four kinds of manifold conditions.
This answer must necessarily possess the meaning of being a true conditionality; by virtue of that meaning of conditionality, regarding the other [factors] grasped as distinct...

Regarding the statement that "the object is also commonly accepted [as such]": this means that because internal consciousness arises by taking an external meaning as its condition (*ālambana*), one also commonly accepts the external atom (*paramāṇu*) as the objective field.
However, since atoms cannot produce consciousness, how much less could they be commonly accepted [as such]?

How could it be that the internal image-part (*nimittabhāga*) truly produces consciousness while itself lacks the status of being an objective condition? It is just like the immediately preceding cessation (*samanantaranirodha*), which is likewise [a condition].

Regarding the statement that "the consciousness which performs the act of discernment (*vikalpa*) is that which functions as a cutter": this refers to the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

It does not mean that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is induced [simultaneously] with the five sensory consciousnesses. As for "cutter," this signifies the distinct, non-common intentionality of these five consciousnesses.

That is to say, even if these five consciousnesses lack a simultaneous mental consciousness, they themselves possess four kinds of multiple conditions; how then could they be devoid of an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?
Thus ends the *Commentary on the Exposition of the Object-Condition* (*Ālambanaparīkṣā-vyākhyā*).
[Question and Answer Clarifications to the Commentary on the Exposition of the Object-Condition.]
Question: For what reason was this *Ālambanapratyayaparīkṣā* (Treatise on the Object-condition) composed? Answer: To clarify internal and external form (*rūpa*). What is called external form?

It refers to that which other schools take to be the objects of the five consciousnesses as the aggregation of atoms (*paramāṇu*), as well as what ordinary people perceive as the body, the sense organs, and the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
All [of these] maintain that objects exist outside the mind; therefore, they are called "external forms" (*bāhyarūpa*). How is this known? It is said:

The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states, "Because it is commonly accepted by worldly convention that objects abide externally," and thus it is known. Question: Since atoms aggregate and manifest from the transformation of the mind, they do not depart from the mind at all.
Why, then, are they called "outside the mind"? Answer: They maintain that objects exist outside the mind as distinct entities.
They truly exist; therefore, they are called "external to the mind. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:

"Those who wish to maintain that the five consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness, take external forms (*rūpa*) as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), either hold that atoms (*paramāṇu*) exist as substantial entities because they can produce consciousness, or they hold that there are composites (*saṃghāta*), because when consciousness arises, it bears the aspect (*nimitta*) of those [forms].
This is the attachment to the meaning of externality. Question: What is meant by "internal form"? Answer: It is precisely...

The first five consciousnesses take as their objects the domains of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and when the sixth consciousness does not engage in conceptualization, these are termed "internal matter" (*adhyātma-rūpa*). Question:

Since external matter has as its substance the aggregation of atoms (*paramāṇu*) as well as the sense organs, the body, and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), how do you establish internal matter?
What constitutes its essence? The answer is: it takes as its essence the very same root-body and the vessel-world perceived by worldly people.

When worldly people see a mountain, they give rise to the conceptualization of solidity and establish the name "mountain. When they see water, they give rise to the conceptualization of movement and establish the name "water.
All of these are instances where the mental consciousness falsely discriminates the vessel-world as existing outside of the mind. The same applies to the root-body. If...

The first five consciousnesses take mountains, rivers, and so forth as their objects, yet they do not give rise to the conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) of "mountains, rivers," and so on. Although there are objects present before them, they do not give rise to the conceptualization of "presence.

They clearly perceive various objects, yet they do not give rise to the conceptualization of "perception. Their apprehension of objects is clear and lucid, yet there is no conceptualization of "clarity and lucidity.

Since none of these conceptualizations arise, mind and object are not differentiated; therefore, it is called "internal form" (*adhyātma-rūpa*). The *Śāstra* states: "In this context, the term 'internal' is used to reveal..."

It is not separate from consciousness, yet it possesses an object of perception. Furthermore, it is said: "In this context, the term 'internal' refers to that which is not separate from consciousness;

since there is fundamentally no external [object], in relation to what could something be internal? Thus, one knows that form has neither interior nor exterior, as it is only through the distinctions of the perceiving consciousness that such differences arise.

The designations "internal" and "external" are established as follows. When the first five consciousnesses perceive mountains, rivers, and so forth through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they do not grasp them as being external;

thus, these mountains, rivers, and so forth are termed "internal form. However, when the sixth consciousness perceives mountains, rivers, and so forth, it gives rise to the appearances of mountains, rivers, and so forth from that [consciousness], grasping them as existing externally;
thus, these mountains, rivers, and so forth are termed "external form. Question: What is meant by "contemplation"?

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): it is said that "view" refers to the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*), which is the mind that acts as the subject; "object" (*artha*) refers to the image-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*), which is the objective sphere that serves as the condition;
and "conditioning" (*pratyaya*) refers to the cognitive capacity arising within the image-portion, which is termed the "ultimate sense-faculty" (*paramārthendriya*).

The *Mūla-śāstra* states: "The superior functional capacity (*śakti*) upon consciousness is appropriately termed the five faculties. This capacity and the objective form have served as mutual causes for one another since beginningless time. It should be understood accordingly.

One knows that the five ultimate sense faculties (*paramārtha-indriya*) pervade all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), unlike the superficial sense organs (*tuccha-indriya*), which are restricted to a single physical form.

Since they are called "ultimate," their essence is *tathatā* (suchness). Therefore, it is said that *tathatā* pervades all phenomena; this is precisely the Mahāyāna doctrine of the "Mind-Only nature of all phenomena" (*sarvadharma-vijñaptimātratā*).
Question: If they are called "all phenomena," why are they termed "mind-only"? Answer: It means that when perceiving an object, there is no conceptualization (*vikalpa-saṃjñā*); it is the mind...

The object is one and the same; it is all phenomena (*dharmas*), which are fundamentally quiescent from the beginning. Is this not precisely the fact that the essence of things is mind-only? Question:

In the *Ālambanaparīkṣā* (Treatise on the Investigation of the Object-Condition), recent commentators have generally made no mention of inference (*anumāna*). Why, then, does your current commentary frequently speak of inference? Answer:

There are originally two ways of explaining the meaning of texts in the Western Regions (India). When interpreting sūtras and śāstras, they employ the six-fold analysis (*ṣaḍvidha-vibhāga*). However...

Combined Explanation: If one were to refute the externalist attachments, one would employ a three-membered syllogism (*trirūpa-anumāna*). Now, in composing this root treatise (*mūla-śāstra*), because the purpose is to refute externalist attachments, two syllogisms are established within the treatise.

Dharmapāla explains them as follows. The first syllogism states: The atom (*paramāṇu*) [the subject, *pūrvapakṣa-dharmin*], with respect to the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), is not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) even if it serves as a causal condition (*pratyaya*) [the thesis, *sādhya*].
Because its aspect (*ākāra*) does not exist in the consciousness [the reason, *hetu*]. Just like the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) and so forth [the example, *dṛṣṭānta*]. Next...

The *Pramāṇa* states: "Regarding the preceding subject (the composite entity), it is not the case that the five consciousnesses have an object of cognition (*ālambana*) which is not a causal condition (*pratyaya*).

This is because its substance does not truly exist, just like a second moon. Question: The root treatise says, "If this and that follow one another in terms of existence and non-existence," what is the meaning of this statement?

Answer: "This" refers to the five consciousnesses; "that" refers to the five sense organs. "Existence" refers to their manifest activity (*pravṛtti*), while "non-existence" refers to their seeds (*bīja*).
This means that consciousness and its faculties both possess seeds and manifest forms, yet they are not separate from one another; this is the meaning of "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra).
